definition: Teams whose members are geographically dispersed across different locations, time zones, and often countries.
extendedDefinition: Distributed teams operate across multiple offices, time zones, and countries, relying on software to collaborate as if they shared a room. The core challenges are communication latency, asynchronous handoffs, and cultural differences in working hours. Successful distributed organizations standardize tooling for messaging, video calls, project tracking, and document collaboration, because unplanned sprawl between these systems creates coordination overhead. Clear written communication becomes the default: decisions, meeting notes, and status updates are captured where the whole team can find them. Software buyers supporting distributed work should evaluate async-first features such as recorded meetings, threaded updates, and notification policies that respect time zones. Onboarding also changes in distributed teams, so tools with structured checklists and documentation help new hires ramp up without constant synchronous hand-holding.
examples: A team documents decisions and owners so colleagues in another time zone can continue without waiting for a meeting.
A manager checks whether notifications can be tuned to local working hours and urgent versus routine requests.
A buyer tests how permissions and shared files behave for employees, contractors and external partners in different regions.
description: Distributed teams work across locations and time zones; evaluate software for clear handoffs, access, documentation, coordination and asynchronous work.
